summary: Outlines what AppleTalk's Name Binding Protocol (NBP) did and the properties needed in an IP-based replacement. It reflects a goal of the authors of Multicast DNS and DNS-Based Service Discovery: to retire AppleTalk and NBP. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Old Apple computers used AppleTalk to find printers and shared things nearby. This memo lists what a modern replacement must be able to do.

questions: requirements for replacing nbp with mdns
subtitle: What AppleTalk's Name Binding Protocol did, and what an IP-based replacement had to do at least as well.

tldr.problem: AppleTalk NBP let devices find named services such as printers with no configuration, and IP had no equivalent for name-to-address lookup and service discovery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains what NBP did and lists 15 requirements for an IP-based replacement, from efficient name lookup and typed names to conflict detection and live browsing.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational background document. The RFC says Multicast DNS and DNS-Based Service Discovery together describe a solution that meets these requirements.

today: RFC 6760 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is background for the solution described in RFC 6762 and RFC 6763.

sections.title: Why Replace NBP
sections.content:
An important goal of the people working on Zeroconf, Multicast DNS and DNS-Based Service Discovery was a viable IP-based replacement for AppleTalk and its Name Binding Protocol (NBP). Many DNS experts know nothing about NBP, so this document gives the background behind those design decisions.

Most requirements restate what NBP does, but matching NBP is only a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The replacement should use Unicode in the form of UTF-8 rather than Apple Extended ASCII, and should avoid NBP's reputation, partly deserved, for being too chatty on the network. The RFC says RFC 6762 and RFC 6763, taken together, meet these requirements.
sections.eli5: Before building a new tool, you write down what the old tool did well and what it did badly. This memo is that list.

sections.title: Zero Configuration Networking
sections.content:
TCP/IP traditionally needed configuration, either by a human or by a DHCP server. AppleTalk worked with neither, even with just two laptops joined by a cable or wirelessly. IP now has self-assigned link-local addresses (RFC 3927, RFC 4862), so what remains missing is Zero Configuration name-to-address translation and service discovery.

The three areas (addressing, naming, service discovery) need not all be used together. A network can use conventional unicast DNS for web sites and Multicast DNS for peers on the local link at the same time, so Zeroconf protocols must coexist with configured networks. With no operator to fix problems, they must be self-correcting and keep converging to correctness.
sections.eli5: You plug two computers together and they just work, with nobody typing in settings. The protocols have to fix their own mistakes, because no grown-up is there to help.

sections.title: Naming and Addressing Requirements
sections.content:
NBP's primary function is translating names to addresses, not browsing. Every print job does a simple name-to-address lookup, so a replacement needs an efficient lookup operation as its primary function.

NBP names services, not hardware, because you always talk to software running on a machine. A DNS lookup gives only an IP address, so the port number must be learned some other way, which makes it hard to run several instances of a service on one machine. In AppleTalk each print queue was its own independently named service with its own socket number. A replacement must return the port and any extra demultiplexing information, such as an lpr print queue name, and must name each print queue as a first-class entity. DNS SRV records give a port but cannot give an lpr print queue name.

The text also notes that port numbers are a finite resource: ports 0-49151 are now reserved, leaving only 25% of the space for dynamic allocation.
sections.eli5: An address that only names the building is not enough to deliver a letter. You also need the room number, and each room, like each print queue, should have its own name.

sections.title: Typed, Friendly and Conflict-Free Names
sections.content:
NBP names are written Name : Type @ Zone. The Type is an opaque identifier for the application protocol the service speaks, and the Zone is an organizational or geographical grouping. Each {Type,Zone} pair is its own name space, so a printer called "Sales" and a file server called "Sales" do not conflict. A replacement must offer zones and an independent name space per service type.

Service names are picked from lists, so they should be rich text such as "3rd Floor Copy Room", likely as UTF-8, and must allow any character, including dots and spaces. Since no administrator is assumed, users must be able to name devices freely, which can cause conflicts such as two printers shipped as "Brother Printer". The replacement must detect conflicts continuously, not just at boot. A laptop should tell its user to choose a new name, while a printer without a screen should pick one automatically, for example "Brother Printer 2".

If the scheme is integrated with global DNS, a sub-tree of that name space should be designated local-only, much as RFC 1918 does for addresses.
sections.eli5: Each kind of thing gets its own list of names, so a printer and a file server can both be called Sales. If two printers pick the same name, one quietly becomes Printer 2.

sections.title: Browsing, Binding and Behaviour
sections.content:
Remaining requirements cover how the protocol behaves:

  • Late binding: store only the name, and look up the current address and port each time the service is used.
  • Simplicity: simple enough for the firmware of a low-cost ink-jet printer.
  • Browsing: list all instances of a service type in a zone, like NBP's wild-card name =.
  • Guidance: tell clients the suggested and available zones for registering and for browsing.
  • Power management: discover services on sleeping devices and wake them when needed.
  • Protocol agnostic: not tied to a language or data format.
  • Cache coherency: any caching needs a way to handle stale data.
  • Live results: a browse list should appear within one second and update as things change, without a Refresh button.
sections.eli5: Look up where your friend lives each time you visit, because they might have moved. Show the list of friends straight away, and keep it up to date by itself.

sections.title: Existing Protocols, IPv6 and Security
sections.content:
The RFC answers the recurring question of whether the Service Location Protocol (SLP, RFC 2608) is the IETF replacement for NBP. It says SLP is rich in browsing but provides none of the service naming, automatic conflict detection or efficient name-to-address lookup that make up most of NBP, and that it offers far more mechanism than needed for browsing. SLP returns URLs, which are not useful without DNS names.

A replacement needs to support IPv6 as well as IPv4. On security, NBP was developed when little thought was given to it, so a modern replacement should have measures suited to its environment. The document specifies no protocol, so it leaves details out.
sections.eli5: Another tool already existed, but it did only one of the jobs. This section explains why it was not enough, and says the new tool should be safe and work with both kinds of address.

viz.caption: A SELECTION OF THE 15 REQUIREMENTS IN RFC 6760

items.title: Name-to-address
items.text: An efficient lookup is the primary function.

items.title: Services, not hardware
items.text: Name the software service, not the machine.

items.title: Typed name space
items.text: Each type and zone pair has its own names.

items.title: Conflict detection
items.text: Ongoing detection, not only at boot.

items.title: Late binding
items.text: Store the name; look up address and port at use.

items.title: Live browsing
items.text: Results within one second, updated as things change.
